newsitem.title: UK: British toy shops have disappointing Christmas.
newsitem.headline: British toy shops have disappointing Christmas.

text.p: Less than sparkling reports on Christmas trading from two toy retailers on Thursday suggested the British toy market was no fun this year, with competition very tough and demand softer than expected.
Hamleys Plc said Christmas trading this year was disappointing, while intense competition squeezed sales and margins at John Menzies Plc's toy shop chain Early Learning Centre.

Hamleys, whose flagship store is on London's Regent Street, said Christmas sales started well in the first week of December, but tailed off in the middle of the month and only recovered significantly during the Christmas week.
Finance director Michael Riddy said, "Overall we were a little disappointed with Christmas."
He told Reuters in a telephone interview the toy market had not been great this December and Regent Street itself had been quieter than last year.

Retail analysts agreed that toys were difficult, saying catalogue showroom retailer Argos Plc had not done so well on toys, while the strong performance from Kingfisher Plc's Woolworths chain was driven by aggressive promotions.
Hamleys, which describes itself as "The finest toy shop in the world", said sales were up 3.6 percent in the five months from August to December 1996.

Sales from its House of Toys concession in department store group House of Fraser Plc were 8.7 percent below last year due to the smaller number of concessions trading and the repositioning of some of the sites.
Riddy said Hamleys' bestseller was Buzz Lightyear, the character from the film Toy Story, but sales did not match those of Power Rangers a couple of years ago.
Distribution and retailing group John Menzies suffered a fall in toy sales. It reported lower Christmas sales and half year profits, and warned that full year profits would not make up the shortfall.
Its Early Learning Centre toy shops, which cater for children aged 0 to five, found competition had hotted up in the past 12 to 18 months.
"Two years ago we had the field to ourselves," managing director David Mackay told Reuters, "We now have intense competition from Woolworths, Argos, Boots and Toys R Us."
Plans to fight back included rolling out a new format store being tested in London and Bromley in Kent, plus extending the range to appeal to children aged five to 10.
John Menzies' half year pretax profit fell to 2.6 million pounds ($4.35 million) from 3.8 million, while sales rose to 645.6 million pounds from 628.4 million. The dividend was held at 4.8 pence.
Hamleys shares stood five pence higher at 372.5 pence, while John Menzies tumbled 60 pence to 485 pence. ($1=.5976 Pound)
